title: Not Every Debt Can Be Settled Through Compensation
deck: Being unable to restore things does not mean we may erase the past, nor that the past may govern the whole future.
body: After causing a loss, people naturally look for ways to compensate.
A damaged object can be replaced, spent resources can be returned, and lost time may be made up for through new arrangements. Compensation takes responsibility beyond an “I’m sorry” and into reality.
But not every debt can be settled through compensation.
Once some things have happened, the previous state no longer exists.
A disclosed secret cannot become unknown again; a missed opportunity cannot be guaranteed to return; damaged trust cannot be put back in its place like an object.
Compensation still matters here, but it cannot reset the past to zero.
At this point, we often fall into two opposite errors.
One is to think that since compensation has been paid, the matter should be over.

The person responsible has made what they consider reasonable amends and expects the other person to resume their former attitude. If the other remains cautious or unwilling to draw close, they are considered unwilling to move forward.
The other error is to think that since things cannot be restored, the debt can never have a boundary.
Past harm becomes grounds for every later demand. No compensation is enough and no change can be acknowledged, because what was lost really cannot return.
The first approach forces what remains to disappear. The second lets it expand without limit.
Real repair requires rejecting both of these easy conclusions.
Compensation must first face the specific loss.

Not “I’ve already done so much,” but: what did the other person actually lose? Which parts can be restored, and which can only be acknowledged? Who needs to bear the burden, and how far does it extend?
Sometimes what the person responsible is willing to offer is not what the other person really needs.

They give gifts, arrange a special event, or repeatedly apologize, because these things let them feel they are making repairs. But the other person may need transparent information, changed behavior, the return of their right to choose, or simply permission for the relationship not to go back to what it was.
Compensation cannot be designed solely by the person who caused the loss.
But this does not give the harmed person the power to make every demand automatically reasonable.

Compensation should stay connected to the loss caused by the incident. A breach of trust may call for clearer explanations in the future, but does not automatically entitle the other person to inspect an entire life; a financial loss may call for repayment and covering costs, but does not confer control of all another person’s decisions.
The harm is real, and the scope must be real too.
These limits do not downplay the past; they prevent it from swallowing every possible future.
Some debts can ultimately be borne only incompletely.

The person responsible acknowledges: I cannot fully return what you lost. What I can do is stop denying it, repair as much as possible of what can be repaired, and keep the same pattern from recurring in my later actions.
The harmed person may also need to decide: when full restoration is impossible, how much room am I willing to give this event in the future? Will I continue, keep my distance, or end things?
No choice can make what happened never have happened.
The point of repair is therefore not to restore an untouched starting point.

It is to give the loss that cannot be erased an honest but limited place. It is remembered, informs the relevant judgments, and calls for the corresponding responsibilities. But it need not become the sole explanation for every future interaction.
The phrase “settle the account” can mislead us into thinking every debt in a relationship can be converted into the same unit.
But some things have no equivalent.

New goodwill does not mean old harm never happened; lasting change does not mean the other person must trust again. These can only become new facts, allowing the other person to judge anew in their own time.
Someone taking responsibility may keep changing, but cannot demand that change be exchanged immediately for forgiveness.
Someone who has been hurt may reserve judgment, but cannot use what cannot be returned as grounds for unlimited possession of another person’s future.
Not every debt can be settled.
But being unable to settle does not mean there is nothing to do but pursue repayment forever.
Sometimes the most honest repair is for both people to acknowledge: an irreplaceable gap will always remain here. We will not pretend it is absent, and we will not let it own the whole future.
entry_door: This essay uses no theoretical terms, but behind it lies the same question: how can a relationship draw close to someone without living their life for them? To follow this line of thought further, start with Non Dubito in Five Minutes.
